sources.text: Cardiovascular Risk Reduction with Icosapent Ethyl for Hypertriglyceridemia. BACKGROUND: Patients with elevated triglyceride levels are at increased risk for ischemic events. Icosapent ethyl, a highly purified eicosapentaenoic acid ethyl ester, lowers triglyceride levels, but data are needed to determine its effects on ischemic events. METHODS: We performed a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial involving patients with established cardiovascular disease or with diabetes and other risk factors, who had been receiving statin therapy and who had a fasting triglyceride level of 135 to 499 mg per deciliter (1.52 to 5.63 mmol per liter) and a low-density lipoprotein cholesterol level of 41 to 100 mg per deciliter (1.06 to 2.59 mmol per liter). The patients were randomly assigned to receive 2 g of icosapent ethyl twice daily (total daily dose, 4 g) or placebo. The primary end point was a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, coronary revascularization, or unstable angina. The key secondary end point was a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke. RESULTS: A total of 8179 patients were enrolled (70.7% for secondary prevention of cardiovascular events) and were followed for a median of 4.9 years. A primary end-point event occurred in 17.2% of the patients in the icosapent ethyl group, as compared with 22.0% of the patients in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.75; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.68 to 0.83; P<0.001); the corresponding rates of the key secondary end point were 11.2% and 14.8% (hazard ratio, 0.74; 95% CI, 0.65 to 0.83; P<0.001). The rates of additional ischemic end points, as assessed according to a prespecified hierarchical schema, were significantly lower in the icosapent ethyl group than in the placebo group, including the rate of cardiovascular death (4.3% vs. 5.2%; hazard ratio, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.66 to 0.98; P=0.03). A larger percentage of patients in the icosapent ethyl group than in the placebo group were hospitalized for atrial fibrillation or flutter (3.1% vs. 2.1%, P=0.004). Serious bleeding events occurred in 2.7% of the patients in the icosapent ethyl group and in 2.1% in the placebo group (P=0.06). CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with elevated triglyceride levels despite the use of statins, the risk of ischemic events, including cardiovascular death, was significantly lower among those who received 2 g of icosapent ethyl twice daily than among those who received placebo. (Funded by Amarin Pharma; REDUCE-IT ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT01492361 .).

Abstract Background The efficacy of icosapent ethyl among patients with very well‐controlled baseline low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL‐C) is unknown. Methods In this post hoc analysis of the REDUCE‐IT (Reduction of Cardiovascular Events With Icosapent Ethyl–Intervention Trial) randomized clinical trial, statin‐treated patients with high cardiovascular risk, elevated triglycerides (135–499 mg/dL), and baseline LDL‐C of 41 to 100 mg/dL were included. Patients were randomized to icosapent ethyl (2 g twice daily) or placebo and then post hoc stratified by baseline LDL‐C (<55 mg/dL versus ≥55 mg/dL). The primary composite end point included cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, coronary revascularization, or unstable angina. Results Among 8175 patients with baseline LDL‐C data, 7117 (87.1%) had LDL‐C ≥55 mg/dL and 1058 (12.9%) had LDL‐C <55 mg/dL. In patients with LDL‐C <55 mg/dL, the rate of the primary composite end point was lower in the icosapent ethyl group (16.2% versus 22.8%) than in the placebo group (hazard ratio [HR], 0.66 [95% CI, 0.50–0.87]; absolute risk reduction, 6.6%; P =0.003). Among patients with LDL‐C ≥55 mg/dL, a primary composite end point event occurred in a lower proportion of patients in the icosapent ethyl group (17.4% versus 21.9%) than in the placebo group (HR, 0.76 [95% CI, 0.69–0.85]; absolute risk reduction, 4.5%; P <0.0001). No significant interaction was observed between baseline LDL‐C and treatment group ( P for interaction=0.40). Findings were consistent among secondary cardiovascular end points and in sensitivity analyses. Conclusions Among statin‐treated patients with elevated triglycerides and high cardiovascular risk, icosapent ethyl reduced the rate of cardiovascular end points irrespective of baseline LDL‐C, including among eligible patients with optimal LDL‐C control. In this post hoc analysis of REDUCE‐IT (Reduction of Cardiovascular Events With Icosapent Ethyl–Intervention Trial), 8175 statin‐treated patients with high cardiovascular risk and elevated triglycerides were randomized to icosapent ethyl or placebo and then stratified by baseline low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol control (<55 mg/dL versus ≥55 mg/dL). Icosapent ethyl significantly reduced the primary composite end point of cardiovascular events by 34% among patients with very well‐controlled low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol. Findings were consistent across the full range of baseline low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol levels and for a variety of cardiovascular outcomes. What Are the Clinical Implications? Icosapent ethyl is effective in reducing cardiovascular events among indicated patients irrespective of baseline low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol. Icosapent ethyl should be considered for statin‐treated patients with elevated triglycerides and high cardiovascular risk even if low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol is optimally controlled. Patients with mildly to moderately elevated triglycerides have an increased risk of cardiovascular disease. , Icosapent ethyl is a purified eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) ethyl ester that has been shown to decrease triglyceride levels, in addition to favorable effects on plasma levels of oxidized low‐density lipoproteins, various plasma markers of inflammation, and cell membrane stabilization. , , , , The REDUCE‐IT (Reduction of Cardiovascular Events With Icosapent Ethyl–Intervention Trial) randomized clinical trial demonstrated that statin‐treated patients with low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL‐C) of ≤100 mg/dL, elevated triglycerides (135–499 mg/dL), and high cardiovascular risk experienced fewer cardiovascular end points with icosapent ethyl compared with placebo. , , , , , , , Recent evidence indicates benefit of intensive LDL‐C lowering, with guidelines recommending an LDL‐C goal of ≤55 mg/dL in especially high‐risk patients. , Whether the beneficial effects of icosapent ethyl are consistent across a range of baseline LDL‐C levels, especially among those with very well‐controlled LDL‐C, remains unknown. Because the triglyceride and cholesterol pathways have substantial overlap, evaluating treatment heterogeneity among drugs targeting these markers is important. Understanding if icosapent ethyl reduces cardiovascular events in patients with optimal LDL‐C on statin therapy can inform therapy decisions. We performed a post hoc secondary analysis of REDUCE‐IT to determine the efficacy of icosapent ethyl compared with placebo for cardiovascular event reduction among patients stratified by baseline LDL‐C. Methods Study Design and Patient Population Patients in REDUCE‐IT were included. REDUCE‐IT has been described previously. , In brief, REDUCE‐IT was a double‐blind, randomized, placebo‐controlled trial enrolling patients from 473 sites in 11 countries. Randomization occurred between November 28, 2011, and August 4, 2016. Patients were randomized to icosapent ethyl (2 g twice daily with food) or placebo. Patients aged ≥45 years with cardiovascular disease or ≥50 years with diabetes and ≥1 cardiovascular risk factor were included. Patients were further selected to be on statin treatment consistently for at least 4 weeks. Patients were included if they had triglycerides of 135 to 499 mg/dL and LDL‐C of 41 to 100 mg/dL. Patients were excluded if they had severe heart failure, acute severe liver disease, or a glycated hemoglobin >10.0%. Other key inclusion and exclusion criteria, as well as detailed methods and protocol, have been described previously. The data that support the findings and the methods used to conduct the study may be made available upon reasonable request to the corresponding author. For this analysis, patients were stratified by baseline LDL‐C to <55 mg/dL or ≥55 mg/dL. This threshold was consistent with the LDL‐C target for patients with cardiovascular disease by the European Society of Cardiology guidelines. In sensitivity analyses (see Statistical Analysis section), patients were stratified by LDL‐C <70 mg/dL and ≥70 mg/dL, as this threshold was consistent with American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association guidelines for lipid control. These thresholds were selected to stratify patients to well‐controlled and less‐controlled LDL‐C groups. Baseline LDL‐C was determined as the last nonmissing measurement of LDL‐C before randomization. LDL‐C was obtained via preparative ultracentrifugation. If not available by preparative ultracentrifugation, then another LDL‐C value before randomization was obtained, preferably by direct measurement of LDL‐C, and if not available, then by Friedewald calculation (for patients with triglycerides <400 mg/dL) or otherwise by the Martin–Hopkins equation. , Outcomes The primary composite end point included cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction (MI), nonfatal stroke, coronary revascularization, or unstable angina. Multiple secondary end points were studied: cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, or nonfatal stroke (termed key secondary composite end point); cardiovascular death or nonfatal MI; fatal or nonfatal MI; urgent or emergent revascularization; cardiovascular death; hospitalization for unstable angina; fatal or nonfatal stroke; all‐cause death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke; and all‐cause death. Safety end points included a composite of treatment‐emergent adverse events (TEAEs), including severe TEAEs and drug‐related TEAEs, as well as cause‐specific TEAE (ie, atrial fibrillation/atrial flutter). Statistical Analysis After stratifying patients by baseline LDL‐C (<55 mg/dL or ≥55 mg/dL), end points were assessed by treatment group with intention‐to‐treat analyses for time to first event. Log‐rank P values were reported from Kaplan–Meier analysis, stratified by geographic region, cardiovascular risk category (established cardiovascular disease or diabetes plus risk factors), and use of ezetimibe. Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% CIs were determined using a Cox proportional hazards model computed to determine the risk of the primary and key secondary end points according to the use of icosapent ethyl compared with placebo. To assess heterogeneity in treatment effects, interaction analyses were performed. In these analyses, differences by baseline LDL‐C group were examined with Cox proportional hazard models including an interaction term for baseline LDL‐C group and treatment group. Heterogeneity in the relative treatment effect was assessed by evaluating continuous baseline LDL‐C with a Cox proportional hazard model incorporating treatment assignment, a natural cubic spline of baseline LDL‐C, and the interaction between treatment and the spline. Knots were specified at the 25th percentile, median, and 75th percentile of baseline LDL‐C, and a Wald test was used to assess the significance of the interaction term. To ensure robustness of results, multiple sensitivity analyses were conducted. First, the primary composite end point was determined among patients with cardiovascular disease history. Second, the entire cohort was stratified by a less intensive LDL‐C threshold: LDL‐C <70 mg/dL and LDL‐C ≥70 mg/dL. Four patients were excluded for missing baseline LDL‐C values (<0.05%). A P threshold of <0.05 was considered significant for the overall analyses, and a P threshold of <0.10 was considered significant for the interaction analyses, consistent with prior studies. Analyses were conducted with SAS 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC). REDUCE‐IT was approved by the appropriate institutional review boards, public health authorities, and ethics committees. Informed consent was obtained from participants. REDUCE‐IT was registered on ClinicalTrials.Gov ( NCT01492361 ). Results REDUCE‐IT included 8179 patients. After excluding 4 patients with missing baseline LDL‐C data, the final study population consisted of 8175 patients. Of these patients, 7117 (87.1%) had baseline LDL‐C ≥55 mg/dL, and 1058 (12.9%) had LDL‐C <55 mg/dL. Discussion Icosapent ethyl reduced the rate of cardiovascular outcomes in statin‐treated patients with elevated triglycerides irrespective of baseline LDL‐C. These results were consistent across various secondary cardiovascular outcomes and in multiple sensitivity analyses, including with a different baseline LDL‐C threshold and in patients with cardiovascular disease history. Patients with well‐managed baseline LDL‐C, to levels less than 55 mg/dL, benefited similarly from icosapent ethyl therapy as those with LDL‐C above the target. Icosapent ethyl demonstrated a large 34% reduction in cardiovascular events in patients with baseline LDL‐C <55 mg/dL. Additionally, spline analyses suggested benefits of icosapent ethyl down to the lowest values of baseline LDL‐C (as low as 40 mg/dL). These findings support that icosapent ethyl can prevent many cardiovascular events in patients with elevated triglycerides who are at high cardiovascular event risk. Most contemporary lipid therapies for cardiovascular event prevention have focused on LDL‐C control. , , However, the current study emphasizes that among patients with elevated triglycerides, icosapent ethyl can be an effective additional strategy to further improve cardiovascular outcomes, even among statin‐treated patients achieving excellent LDL‐C control. Prior evidence has shown consistency of icosapent ethyl benefits across statin types, further supporting the independent benefits from LDL‐C control. Our findings suggested a numerically higher risk reduction of the primary outcome in the lower LDL‐C group in comparison with the higher LDL‐C group (34% versus 24%), which could be a marker of improved adherence to both statins and icosapent ethyl. However, these findings are challenging to interpret, as the difference is not statistically significant, and thus should be considered exploratory. Further studies to evaluate if this signal is real are necessary. Despite these compelling findings, and the demonstrated cost effectiveness of icosapent ethyl, , clinical use of icosapent ethyl remains discouragingly low, even in countries where it has been approved and widely available for several years. Concerted efforts to identify and decrease barriers to icosapent ethyl therapy are important for improving cardiovascular outcomes in eligible patients, including any barriers in cost‐related access. Strategies to initiate therapy among indicated patients at index admission for acute coronary syndrome are likely to be effective and warranted. Surveillance data have demonstrated that the prevalence of mild to moderately elevated triglyceride levels in the United States continues to remain high, and icosapent ethyl should be considered to reduce cardiovascular events in such patients who are at high cardiovascular risk. Low adoption could also reflect current clinical uncertainty for whether very low LDL‐C itself lessens residual risk in this population and, if not, whether icosapent ethyl continues to lower risk across a range of cardiovascular outcomes at such low LDL‐C levels. Our findings indicate that icosapent ethyl has beneficial effects independent of the many known contributions of LDL‐C to atherosclerosis. Icosapent ethyl is known to improve triglyceride levels, with REDUCE‐IT demonstrating 20% reduction in triglycerides with therapy. While the cardiovascular benefits of icosapent ethyl therapy might be in some part secondary to triglyceride lowering, data from REDUCE‐IT strongly suggest that other mechanisms are likely significant contributors. In addition to triglyceride control, higher EPA levels can lead to cardiovascular benefit. Analyses of REDUCE‐IT showed no difference in cardiovascular event reduction with icosapent ethyl whether the on‐treatment triglyceride levels were above or below 150 mg/dL. Importantly, in addition to this finding within REDUCE‐IT, the STRENGTH (Long‐Term Outcomes Study to Assess Statin Residual Risk With Epanova in High Cardiovascular Risk Patients With Hypertriglyceridemia) trial, which tested mixed EPA plus docosahexaenoic acid (omega‐3), and the PROMINENT (Pemafibrate to Reduce Cardiovascular Outcomes by Reducing Triglycerides in Patients With Diabetes) trial, which tested pemafibrate, showed lack of improvement in cardiovascular outcomes with triglyceride lowering among patients with hypertriglyceridemia. , Similar findings were observed among trials assessing niacin for triglyceride lowering. , , Thus, non–triglyceride‐related mechanisms are likely important to explain the cardiovascular benefit of icosapent ethyl in REDUCE‐IT. , , Additionally, irrespective of the biomarker pathway, imaging findings in the EVAPORATE (Effect of Vascepa on Improving Coronary Atherosclerosis in People With High Triglycerides Taking Statin Therapy) trial showed that icosapent ethyl led to a reduction in low‐attenuation plaque on coronary computed tomography angiography. Coronary plaque regression has been associated with improvement in cardiovascular outcomes and may be the pathway leading to beneficial effects with icosapent ethyl. Similar to REDUCE‐IT, the JELIS (Japan EPA Lipid Intervention Study) trial showed benefits with EPA, with the latter study including patients with hyperlipidemia and increased inflammatory state. In subgroup analyses, JELIS demonstrated no significant heterogeneity in treatment effect when stratifying patients by a LDL‐C threshold of ≈180 mg/dL (4.7 mmol/L). Our study adds evidence for the beneficial effects of EPA among those with much lower LDL‐C levels. Similarly, the RESPECT‐EPA (Randomized Trial for Evaluation in Secondary Prevention Efficacy of Combination Therapy–Statin and Eicosapentaenoic Acid) trial suggested improved cardiovascular outcomes with icosapent ethyl among patients with chronic coronary artery disease. RESPECT‐EPA subgroup analyses showed consistent benefit with EPA when patients were stratified by baseline LDL‐C of 70 mg/dL. REDUCE‐IT, JELIS, and RESPECT‐EPA, when compared with STRENGTH, used higher‐dose EPA formulations, , , with evidence indicating a relationship between EPA and cardiovascular outcome reduction. , , Although expected, it is reassuring to note that TEAE rates were similar by baseline LDL‐C group as for the overall trial, without significant differences in severe TEAEs or drug‐related TEAEs. It is also important to note that increased rates of atrial fibrillation or flutter, and a trend toward increased rates of serious adverse event bleeding were observed with icosapent ethyl in both LDL‐C strata, though absolute risk differences for serious adverse event bleeding were low in both cases. Overall, these findings continue to suggest the safety of icosapent ethyl as seen in prior REDUCE‐IT publications, although physicians will need to consider possible adverse effects when prescribing therapy. We acknowledge the limitations of the analyses presented. First, this study was a post hoc analysis. Second, randomization was not stratified by baseline LDL‐C, though reassuringly we found that baseline characteristics were similar among the different baseline LDL‐C study groups. Third, REDUCE‐IT patients had very low use of ezetimibe and PCSK9 inhibitors. Fourth, REDUCE‐IT only enrolled patients with well‐controlled or mild to moderate elevations of LDL‐C (LDL‐C ≤100 mg/dL). In conclusion, icosapent ethyl reduced the rate of cardiovascular events among statin‐treated patients with high cardiovascular risk and elevated triglycerides, irrespective of baseline LDL‐C. The large and statistically significant reduction in cardiovascular end points with icosapent ethyl in patients with LDL‐C <55 mg/dL suggests that this agent should also be considered for cardiovascular event prevention in statin‐treated patients with elevated cardiovascular risk despite well‐controlled LDL‐C. Abstract Background In REDUCE‐IT (Reduction of Cardiovascular Events With Icosapent Ethyl–Intervention Trial), icosapent ethyl (IPE) versus placebo) reduced cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, coronary revascularization, or unstable angina requiring hospitalization, but was associated with increased atrial fibrillation/atrial flutter (AF) hospitalization (3.1% IPE versus 2.1% placebo; P =0.004). Methods and Results We performed post hoc efficacy and safety analyses of patients with or without prior AF (before randomization) and with or without in‐study time‐varying AF hospitalization to assess relationships of IPE (versus placebo) and outcomes. In‐study AF hospitalization event rates were higher in patients with prior AF (12.5% versus 6.3%, IPE versus placebo; P =0.007) versus without prior AF (2.2% versus 1.6%, IPE versus placebo; P =0.09). Serious bleeding rates trended higher in patients with (7.3% versus 6.0%, IPE versus placebo; P =0.59) versus without prior AF (2.3% versus 1.7%, IPE versus placebo; P =0.08). With IPE, serious bleeding trended higher regardless of prior AF (interaction P value [ P int ]=0.61) or postrandomization AF hospitalization ( P int =0.66). Patients with prior AF (n=751, 9.2%) versus without prior AF (n=7428, 90.8%) had similar relative risk reductions of the primary composite and key secondary composite end points with IPE versus placebo ( P int =0.37 and P int =0.55, respectively). Conclusions In REDUCE‐IT, in‐study AF hospitalization rates were higher in patients with prior AF especially in those randomized to IPE. Although serious bleeding trended higher in those randomized to IPE versus placebo over the course of the study, serious bleeding was not different regardless of prior AF or in‐study AF hospitalization. Patients with prior AF or in‐study AF hospitalization had consistent relative risk reductions across primary, key secondary, and stroke end points with IPE. Nonstandard Abbreviations and Acronyms IPE icosapent ethyl MACE major adverse cardiac event OAC oral anticoagulant REDUCE‐IT Reduction of Cardiovascular Events With Icosapent Ethyl–Intervention Trial Clinical Perspective What Is New? Patients in REDUCE‐IT (Reduction of Cardiovascular Events With Icosapent Ethyl–Intervention Trial) had greater risk of hospitalization for atrial fibrillation/atrial flutter (AF) in the icosapent ethyl (IPE) versus the placebo arm. Risk of hospitalization for AF with IPE did not differ statistically between patients with baseline history of AF before randomization compared with those without a baseline history of AF. Risk of serious bleeding with IPE trended insignificantly higher than with placebo for those randomized with and without baseline history of AF. What Are the Clinical Implications? Point estimates for cardiovascular benefit (primary and key secondary composite cardiovascular end points and individual end point components) with IPE were statistically similar despite presence or absence of baseline history of AF. Atrial fibrillation, particularly in patients with or at risk for coronary artery disease, is associated with increased risk of adverse outcomes including debilitating symptoms, worsening myocardial ischemia, stroke, heart failure, hypertension, and ultimately, death. Patients with atrial fibrillation may be at greater risk of bleeding because of oral anticoagulation prescribed to reduce thromboembolic events in these patients. Recent meta‐analytic data suggest that omega‐3 fatty acids increase risk of atrial fibrillation, but risk appears minimal or absent in some reports. Surprisingly, some published meta‐analyses include results from REDUCE‐IT (Reduction of Cardiovascular Events With Icosapent Ethyl–Intervention Trial) that, until now, have not been reported fully. Risk of atrial fibrillation with omega‐3 fatty acids and subsequent outcomes may depend upon underlying comorbidities, specific omega‐3 formulation and dose, and concomitant medications. In selected populations, randomized controlled clinical trials of omega‐3 fatty acids have generally been unable to show benefit in reducing atrial arrhythmias, , , but open‐label trials suggest benefit. Even if omega‐3 fatty acids have antiarrhythmic properties, there may be additional effects on risk of thromboembolic stroke and bleeding. Some reports suggest omega‐3 fatty acids increase risk of bleeding, but data conflict. , , , Icosapent ethyl (IPE), a highly purified form of the omega‐3 fatty acid, eicosapentaenoic acid, has shown remarkable benefits in patients at risk for or who have cardiovascular disease. REDUCE‐IT, , , , , , , , , , , a multinational, double‐blind trial, randomized 8179 statin‐treated patients with controlled low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol, elevated triglycerides, and cardiovascular risk, to IPE 4 g/d or mineral oil placebo and followed patients for a median of 4.9 years. IPE reduced the primary composite end point (cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction [MI], nonfatal stroke, coronary revascularization, or unstable angina requiring hospitalization) by 25% and key secondary end points (cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, or nonfatal stroke) by 26% (each P <0.0001), and reduced individual end points including cardiovascular death (by 20%; P =0.03), stroke (by 28%; P =0.01), MI (by 31%; P <0.001), cardiac arrest (by 48%; P =0.01), and sudden cardiac death (by 31%; P =0.03). Recent evidence from REDUCE‐IT indicates robustness of the data on Clinical End Point Committee adjudication as well as blinded investigator‐reported assessment. However, randomization to IPE was associated with increased risk of atrial fibrillation/atrial flutter (AF) hospitalization versus placebo (3.1% versus 2.1%; P =0.004) as a tertiary adjudicated end point of REDUCE‐IT. Because there was greater risk of hospitalization for AF in patients randomized to IPE versus placebo in REDUCE‐IT, we performed a series of analyses to evaluate relationships of IPE with risk of cardiovascular events and safety in 2 patient cohorts, those with prior AF and those with AF hospitalization during REDUCE‐IT, to explore potential benefit–risk relationships with IPE versus placebo. METHODS The methods of and results from REDUCE‐IT have been published previously. , , , , , , , From these prospective randomized data, we performed post hoc exploratory analyses with a focus on AF. We performed post hoc efficacy and safety analyses of patients with or without prior AF (a baseline history of AF before randomization) and with or without in‐study time‐varying AF hospitalization to assess relationships of IPE (versus placebo) and outcomes. These atrial arrhythmias were not prespecified end points of REDUCE‐IT but were included in a broader prespecified end point category of cardiac arrhythmia requiring hospitalization ≥24 hours. Other incidents of AF not meeting end point criteria were considered adverse events. Electrocardiograms were required annually after randomization but were not mandated to determine presence or absence of AF. There was no protocol requirement to categorize AF as paroxysmal, persistent, or permanent, or to assess either AF burden, associated symptoms, or stroke risk via the CHA 2 DS 2 VASc score. This subgroup analysis was an efficacy and safety assessment of patients with or without baseline history of known AF (prerandomization subgroup) or in‐study AF hospitalization (postrandomization subgroup); because these subgroup analyses were all post hoc, the trial was not powered for their significance. Data from patients who developed AF during the study were not censored. The data that support the findings of this study may be made available from the principal investigator upon reasonable request. The protocol was approved by health authorities, ethics committees and institutional review boards, and participants gave written informed consent. All sites received ethics approval from relevant institutional review boards, and informed consent was obtained. End Points AF before randomization was identified from the medical history. In‐study AF was assessed predominantly via adverse event reporting and was considered present if AF lasted >1 minute resulting in hospitalization (≥24 hours), during or within 24 hours of termination of the last episode, or required continued hospitalization for treatment. If AF was suspected to result in or affect hospitalization, the event was submitted to the Clinical End Point Committee, reviewed by 2 cardiologists blinded to randomized assignments for assessment, and adjudicated. If the adjudicators did not reach consensus, then the Clinical End Point Committee chair made the final determination. Relationships between AF hospitalizations and the primary efficacy end point (composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, coronary revascularization, or unstable angina), key secondary end point (composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, or nonfatal stroke), components of the composite end points, and mortality were assessed in time‐to‐event analyses. Statistical Analysis Analyses were performed according to the intention‐to‐treat principle. Time to first events of clinical end points between IPE and placebo were compared using the log‐rank test estimated from a Kaplan‐Meier analysis and stratified by prespecified factors of cardiovascular risk category, geographic region, and baseline use of ezetimibe. Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% CIs were generated from stratified Cox proportional hazard models. Additionally, a time‐varying covariate of in‐study AF hospitalization was included in a Cox proportional hazard frailty model to estimate HR and 95% CI of the primary efficacy end point for patients with or without in‐study AF. All tests were based on a 2‐sided α level of 5%, with no multiplicity adjustment. All statistical analyses were conducted using SAS version 9.4 software (SAS Institute, Cary, NC). RESULTS Of 8179 randomized patients in REDUCE‐IT, 751 (9.2%) had a baseline history of AF; 7428 (90.8%) did not. After randomization, 211 (2.6%) had in‐study AF hospitalization end points and 7968 (97.4%) did not; only 3 patients with in‐study AF hospitalization had study medication withdrawn because of the AF event. AF hospitalizations were greater in those randomized to IPE versus placebo by an absolute difference of 1% (3.1% versus 2.1%; P =0.004; Figure ). The risk with IPE appeared higher if there was a baseline history of AF (HR, 1.96; P =0.007) versus no known baseline history (HR, 1.33; P =0.09), although the relative risk of in‐study AF hospitalization was not significantly different (interaction P value [ P int ]=0.21) between those with versus without a baseline history of AF. There was a 6.2% absolute increase in AF hospitalization with IPE among those with prior AF but a 0.6% absolute increase in AF among those without prior AF. The absolute risk reduction (IPE versus placebo) for the primary composite end point was 2% in those with versus 5.1% for those without prior AF (Figure ). Patients with prior AF and those with in‐study AF hospitalization were more likely to take oral anticoagulants (OACs) than patients without prior AF and those without in‐study hospitalization (77.8% versus 19.0%, with versus without prior AF; and 91.9% versus 22.6%, with versus without in‐study AF hospitalization) and were more likely to use combinations of antiplatelet drugs and OACs (43.8% versus 16.4%, with versus without prior AF; and 77.7% versus 17.4%, with versus without in‐study AF hospitalization). Most patients with prior AF (98.1%) and all patients with in‐study AF hospitalization (100%) were taking an antithrombotic. OACs reported in REDUCE‐IT were mostly warfarin, enoxaparin, heparin, acenocoumarol, rivaroxaban, and apixaban. Patients were classified to the OAC subgroup if they were prescribed OACs at the time of serious bleeding (ie, when the medication started on or before onset of the serious bleeding event and stopped either within 10 days before bleeding or after the bleeding or if the stop date was missing). There were 368 patients on IPE and 383 patients on placebo who had a history of AF. There were 127 patients on IPE and 84 patients on placebo who had AF during the study (ie, from randomization to the end of the study), and the majority of them also had a history of AF before randomization. There were 449 patients on IPE and 443 patients on placebo who had either a history of or in‐study AF. Rates of serious bleeding and the associated HRs between IPE and placebo were estimated across OAC subgroups for patients with history of AF. Similarly, these statistics were estimated for the expanded cohort of patients with either history of AF or in‐study AF. The results showed that IPE plus an OAC did not seem to have increased the risk of bleeding among those patients who had AF, although there was low statistical power to demonstrate it, attributable to the small number of patients in these subgroups (Figure ). DISCUSSION In REDUCE‐IT, patients randomized to IPE were more likely to be hospitalized for AF than those randomized to placebo. Nevertheless, in REDUCE‐IT, there was relative benefit from IPE versus placebo for the primary composite, the key secondary composite, and individual secondary end points, including stroke, even with this increased risk of AF hospitalization in those randomized to IPE. Although P int values were not significant, the HR point estimates for primary and key secondary composite end points were numerically higher in the prior AF subgroup than in the overall intention‐to‐treat population and those without prior AF subgroup (HR, 0.87 versus HR, 0.75 versus HR, 0.74 for the primary end point, respectively), indicating that benefit parity cannot be established definitively, especially because AF hospitalizations doubled in the prior AF subgroup. Statistical power is lacking in determining whether the findings were equivalent or noninferior. The relative risk of serious bleeding was similar with IPE and placebo in patients with prior AF or in‐study AF hospitalization based on P int values. There was greater risk of AF hospitalization if AF was present before randomization and for patients randomized to IPE. For those with prior AF, the rate of AF hospitalization was 12.5%, almost doubled, compared with placebo (6.3%). The greatest absolute risk associated with IPE for AF hospitalization occurred in the small subgroup (n=751) with prior AF (6.2%). The corresponding absolute risk with IPE for AF hospitalization in the larger subgroup (n=7428) without prior AF was substantially smaller (0.6%). Within the large subgroup without prior AF, the risk–benefit ratio appears favorable, with an absolute risk for AF hospitalization (0.6%) being much smaller than the absolute risk reduction of the primary composite major adverse cardiac event (MACE) end point (5.1%). Within the small subgroup with prior AF, the risk–benefit ratio may be less clear, with the absolute risk for AF hospitalization (6.2%) greater than the absolute risk reduction of the primary composite MACE end point (2.0%). In the overall intention‐to‐treat population, the 1.0% absolute risk for AF hospitalization was outweighed by 4.8% absolute risk reduction of the primary composite MACE end point. The absolute risk for serious bleeding associated with IPE in the small subgroup with prior AF appears higher (1.3%) than the subgroup without prior AF (0.6%), but again, the risk–benefit ratio appears favorable, with the greater (4.8%) absolute risk reduction of the primary MACE end point. Initial experimental data indicated that components of fish oil hold promise to treat atrial arrhythmias. Omega‐3 fatty acids can affect vagal activation, L‐type calcium channels, T‐type calcium channels, , , , , , , , , , , , , , , the sodium‐calcium exchanger, , inhibit sodium current, , , , affect triggered activity, inhibit several potassium currents, , affect connexins, inhibit voltage‐gated potassium (Kv) 1.5 channel, , , , , , , , , , , , , , , and can have anti‐inflammatory , , and antioxidant effects, , , and stabilize lipid membranes. , , Fish oil can prolong left atrial and pulmonary vein effective refractory periods, decrease susceptibility to AF induction, and improve atrial mechanical function to affect electrical and structural remodeling beneficially. , Taken together, , , , , , , , , , , , , , , these effects could be anti‐ or proarrhythmic. With omega‐3 fatty acids as a class, there may be a greater susceptibility to the induction of atrial flutter. The ASCEND (A Study of Cardiovascular Events in Diabetes) study, a large, mail‐based, randomized trial, assessed 1 g of omega‐3 fatty acid supplementation (0.84 g eicosapentaenoic acid plus docosahexaenoic acid) on risk of serious vascular events in people with diabetes but without known atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. In ASCEND, the relative risk of AF in those randomized to omega‐3 fatty acids, based mostly on hospitalizations, was 1.23 (95% CI, 0.98–1.54). However, when all AF events were included, using additional data extracted from linked electronic health records, the relative risk was 1.02 (95% CI, 0.91–1.15; ie, not significant). A goal to assess all incident AF was not possible from our database. Despite antiarrhythmic effects of omega‐3 fatty acids, proarrhythmia may occur in select populations and may be attributable specifically to IPE or to the population studied. It is not possible from our data to determine the cause for the observed increase in AF hospitalizations during REDUCE‐IT or if total AF events were related to IPE. In contrast, omega‐3 fatty acids have not been associated with AF in a generally healthy population. In VITAL (Vitamin D and Omega‐3 Trial), 24 127 participants (mean age 66.7 years, 50.8% women) completed the trial. The primary end point was incident AF, and over a median 5.3 years of treatment and follow‐up, treatment with eicosapentaenoic acid plus docosahexaenoic acid or vitamin D 3 compared with placebo showed no difference in the risk of incident AF. However, elevated risk of AF (not related to hospitalization) with omega‐3 fatty acid supplementation has been reported. In the OMEMI (Omega‐3 Fatty Acids in Elderly With Myocardial Infarction) trial, a study in which monitoring was performed using a handheld single‐lead rhythm monitor for 30 seconds twice daily for 14 days at 12 months into the trial, using an omega‐3 fatty acid formulation including docosahexaenoic acid, AF was present in 7.2% of the treated group versus 4.0% in the placebo group ( P =0.06), and median changes in eicosapentaenoic acid and docosahexaenoic acid were +87% and +16% for treated group versus −13% and −8% in the placebo group and were associated with greater elevation in eicosapentaenoic acid levels. In the STRENGTH (Statin Residual Risk Reduction With Epanova in High CV Risk Patients With Hypertriglyceridemia) trial, using a formulation including docosahexaenoic acid and eicosapentaenoic acid, an increased rate of investigator‐reported new‐onset AF (a prespecified tertiary end point) was seen in the omega‐3 group compared with placebo (2.2% versus 1.3%; HR, 1.69 [95% CI, 1.29–2.21]; nominal P <0.001). Findings from previous randomized controlled clinical trials of omega‐3 fatty acids showed no increased bleeding risk and low risk in a large trial of patients undergoing cardiac surgery. , , , Limitations The subgroup analyses presented herein are post hoc explorations to assess potential risk–benefit relationships with IPE versus placebo. Importantly, REDUCE‐IT was not designed or powered to determine presence of episodes of AF or AF burden, or to evaluate antiarrhythmic or proarrhythmic effects of IPE in a population with or at risk for cardiovascular disease treated with a statin. AF was not prespecified as an efficacy end point of REDUCE‐IT but was adjudicated only if hospitalization occurred. Though these analyses are exploratory, the cardiovascular outcome analyses in subsets with AF hospitalization are admittedly hypothesis generating because of potential postrandomization bias. AF was identified from medical history without an objective approach to define its burden. AF symptoms were not assessed nor was there an attempt to characterize AF as persistent, paroxysmal, permanent, or predominantly flutter or fibrillation. Furthermore, the risks of any treatment directed at AF during REDUCE‐IT remains unknown. No information was gathered on need for, reason for, or length of hospitalization (or relationship to AF), or interventions performed during hospitalization. The mechanistic or causal relationship between AF and IPE remains unknown. Finally, the AF group was small, limiting the ability to draw definitive conclusions. CONCLUSIONS In REDUCE‐IT, most AF hospitalizations occurred in patients with history of AF before enrollment. The absolute risk of developing new AF during the study was small (0.6%), especially compared with the benefit in outcomes with IPE (5.1%). However, for those with prior AF, the risk–benefit ratio was less clear because the absolute increase in risk of AF hospitalization (6.2%) was greater than the absolute reduction in the primary end point (2.0%), although that risk reduction includes lower rates of MI, stroke, and cardiovascular death. A similarity of benefit from IPE on the primary end point appears to be present for those with and without prior AF, although in patients with AF, that benefit needs to be balanced against an increased risk of AF.
